$doc: The story behind a rivalry or trophy game, shown in the game's details under 'The rivalry, deep cut'. Keyed by the two teams' logo ids, sorted and joined with '|' (the same key as the trophy photos). Only facts that were checked against more than one source are written here, with the sources listed; a disputed point says it is disputed. All-time records are NOT stored: they change every season, so the details already show them from the live series data. Add a rivalry by adding an entry here, nothing else.

oklahoma|texas.title: Red River Rivalry
oklahoma|texas.summary: Texas and Oklahoma meet at the Cotton Bowl in Dallas, in the middle of the State Fair of Texas, rather than on either campus.
origin: The first game was in 1900, a 28–2 Texas win.
Since 1932 the game has been played at the Cotton Bowl inside Fair Park in Dallas, during the State Fair of Texas, so it is a neutral-site game even though neither school is in Dallas.

trophy.name: Golden Hat
trophy.text: The State Fair of Texas donated the trophy in 1941, first as a bronze hat. When it was reworked in the 1970s it came out gold, and it has been the Golden Hat since.

moments.text: Oklahoma set the series records for most points and widest margin of victory.

alabama|auburn.title: The Iron Bowl
alabama|auburn.summary: Alabama and Auburn play for the state's bragging rights, and for decades there was no game at all.
origin: The first game was in Birmingham in 1893: Auburn 32, Alabama 22.

After the 1907 game the schools stopped playing over a disagreement, and the series did not resume until 1948. Accounts differ on who gave way: one says the Alabama legislature pushed the schools back together by threatening funding, another says Auburn asked for the game in 1944 and Alabama refused.

moments.title: The Kick Six
moments.text: Tied 28–28, No. 1 Alabama tried a 57-yard field goal with one second left. It fell short, and Auburn's Chris Davis, who usually returned punts and was standing deep in the end zone for exactly this, ran it back 109 yards for a 34–28 win. No. 4 Auburn went on to the SEC Championship Game.

sources.label: Oral history of the Kick Six, Awful Announcing

michigan|minnesota.title: The Little Brown Jug
michigan|minnesota.summary: One of college football's best-known rivalry trophies began as a water jug and a coach's suspicion.
origin: In 1903 Michigan coach Fielding Yost reportedly worried Minnesota might tamper with the team's water, so a student manager bought a jug for the visit. It cost 30 cents.

The game ended 6–6. Michigan left the jug behind, and a Minnesota custodian, Oscar Munson, found it in the visitors' locker room. Minnesota athletic director Louis "Doc" Cooke kept it and made it a trophy.
The trophy series is usually dated from 1909, when Cooke and Yost agreed the winner would keep the jug.

trophy.name: Little Brown Jug
trophy.text: A plain earthenware jug, painted with the score of each game. Several famous details are disputed: that Yost wrote to demand it back, and even whether the jug at the 1903 game was brown (one account says white). The name may come from an 1869 song, 'Little Brown Jug,' by Joseph Winner.

sources.label: The origins of the Little Brown Jug, Bentley Historical Library
A brief history of the Little Brown Jug, Minnesota Daily

army|navy.title: Army–Navy Game
army|navy.summary: The service academies' game, with the Commander-in-Chief's Trophy at stake in a three-way series.
origin: The first game was on November 29, 1890, at West Point: Navy 24, Army 0.
The teams have played every year since 1930; they have missed ten years in all.

trophy.name: Commander-in-Chief's Trophy
trophy.text: Since 1972 the trophy has gone to the winner of the season-long series among Army, Navy and Air Force. Army–Navy is the last of the three games.

mississippi-state|ole-miss.title: The Egg Bowl
mississippi-state|ole-miss.summary: Ole Miss and Mississippi State play for a brass football that is called an egg.
origin: The first game was October 28, 1901, at Mississippi State, where the school was then Mississippi A&M: State won 17–0.

The trophy was proposed by Iota Sigma, an Ole Miss honorary activities fraternity, and first awarded in 1927. It is a regulation-size brass football on a wooden base, and the two schools split its $250 cost. Footballs of the 1920s were rounder and more egg-shaped than today's, which is where 'Golden Egg' comes from.
The first game played for it was November 24, 1927, in Oxford: Ole Miss 20, Mississippi State 12. The trophy has been contested every year since.

trophy.name: Golden Egg
trophy.text: The brass football at the center of the series. Accounts disagree on when the game itself became known as the 'Egg Bowl': one credits a 1979 newspaper piece by sportswriter Tom Patterson, another an earlier Clarion-Ledger spread about two teams that were not going to a bowl game.

sources.label: Why is it called the Egg Bowl? Sports Illustrated
The Golden Egg, Ole Miss Athletics

minnesota|wisconsin.title: Border Battle · Paul Bunyan's Axe
minnesota|wisconsin.summary: The two schools have met since 1890, and their trophy is a lumberjack's axe.
origin: The first game was November 15, 1890: Minnesota 63, Wisconsin 0.
From 1930 the winner kept the Slab of Bacon, which went missing in the early 1940s (it was reportedly found in a storage closet in 1994).

Wisconsin's National 'W' Club created Paul Bunyan's Axe to replace it, naming it for the mythical giant lumberjack. The usual date is 1948, though one researcher argues the first game actually played for the Axe was November 19, 1949, since newspapers from November 1948 do not mention it.

trophy.name: Paul Bunyan's Axe
trophy.text: An axe, named for the mythical giant lumberjack. The original was donated to the College Football Hall of Fame in 2003.

sources.label: How the Axe Came to Be, Wisconsin Athletics
Original Axe donated to the College Football Hall of Fame

iowa|minnesota.title: Floyd of Rosedale
iowa|minnesota.summary: A governors' bet over a pig turned a tense rivalry into one of college football's most famous trophies.
origin: After a heated 1934 game, Minnesota Governor Floyd Olson telegraphed Iowa Governor Clyde Herring to ease the tension, wagering a prize hog from each state on the 1935 game. Herring replied, 'It's a bet.'

Minnesota won, 13–6 in most accounts (CBS News reports 13–7). Herring delivered the Iowa hog, a Hampshire boar from Rosedale Farms in Webster County, to Olson at the Capitol in St. Paul. The pig was named Floyd of Rosedale, for the governor and the farm.
The live pig was not part of later games. Olson had a bronze replica made, and that statue is the trophy. A Des Moines gambling complaint against Herring was dismissed.

trophy.name: Floyd of Rosedale
trophy.text: A bronze pig, awarded to the winner each year since 1935. The real Floyd lived on a farm and reportedly died of cholera about eight months after the bet.

sources.label: Floyd of Rosedale, University of Iowa
Meeting Floyd, the actual pig, University of Iowa
The real history behind Floyd of Rosedale, CBS Minnesota

indiana|purdue.title: The Old Oaken Bucket
indiana|purdue.summary: Indiana and Purdue play for a bucket from an Indiana farm, with a chain that grows every year.
origin: The trophy dates to 1925, when alumni of both schools, Indiana's Clarence Jones and Purdue's Russell Gray, proposed an old oaken bucket, taken from a well somewhere in Indiana, as a trophy that fit the state's rural identity. It is named for Samuel Woodworth's poem 'The Old Oaken Bucket.'
Fritz Ernst of Purdue and Whiley Huddle of Indiana found the bucket on the old Bruner farm, between Kent and Hanover in southern Indiana.

The first game for it, November 21, 1925, in Bloomington, ended 0–0. That tie added the first link to the chain, an 'I–P' link. Since then the winning school adds a block letter to the chain, with the score engraved on the bail.

trophy.name: Old Oaken Bucket
trophy.text: The Purdue and Indiana archives note that accounts differ on exactly how old the bucket is and where it came from.

sources.label: Old Oaken Bucket, Indiana University Archives
The Old Oaken Bucket, Indiana Public Media

notre-dame|usc.title: Notre Dame–USC · Jeweled Shillelagh
notre-dame|usc.summary: A series that began over a conversation between two coaches' wives, with a trophy that collects jewels.
origin: The usual account is that Knute Rockne's wife and USC athletic director Gwynn Wilson's wife talked, and Rockne, who preferred a trip to California to a snowy Nebraska road game, put USC on Notre Dame's schedule on December 4, 1926. A Notre Dame Scholastic history says the true origin is not known for sure and offers another version involving Rockne's ties to Iowa coach Howard Jones.
The Jeweled Shillelagh was unveiled at halftime of the 1952 game by the Notre Dame Alumni Club of Los Angeles.

trophy.name: Jeweled Shillelagh
trophy.text: An Irish club of oak or blackthorn. After each game a jewel is added: a ruby-set Trojan head for each USC win, an emerald-set shamrock for each Notre Dame win. The original was retired and is displayed at Notre Dame (sources give 1989 and 1995 for when); the current one, Shillelagh II, was handmade in County Leitrim, Ireland, in 1997.

sources.label: A short history of the Notre Dame–USC rivalry, Scholastic
The gem behind the Jeweled Shillelagh, WNDU

washington|washington-state.title: The Apple Cup
washington|washington-state.summary: Washington and Washington State have played since 1900, and the trophy changed before the name did.
origin: The first game, in Seattle in 1900 (sources give November 29 or 30), ended in a 5–5 tie.
The series first had a bronze shield, the Governor's Trophy, donated in 1934 by Governor Clarence D. Martin.
The Washington Apple Commission donated the 'Big Apple Trophy' in 1962 or 1963 (sources differ), and the game has been the Apple Cup since.

trophy.name: Apple Cup
trophy.text: A trophy named for the state's apple industry, awarded to the winner each year. Washington is a leading apple-producing state, which is where the name comes from.

sources.label: 125 years of Apple Cup history, The Husky Haul
124 years of the Apple Cup, Daily News

california|stanford.title: The Big Game · The Axe
california|stanford.summary: California and Stanford play for an axe that spent years as a stolen prize before the schools agreed to share it.
origin: The Axe first appeared at a Stanford rally in April 1899, when yell leader Billy Erb brought a lumberman's axe to chop up a straw man in blue and gold. (The rally date is given as April 13 or 14.)
Two days later, at a Cal–Stanford baseball game in San Francisco, Cal students took it, and it stayed in Berkeley for the next 31 years.
In 1930 a group of Stanford students, the 'Immortal 21', took it back; by one account they posed as reporters and used tear gas on its custodian.
After three years of negotiation the schools agreed in 1933 that the Big Game's winner would hold the Axe. A tie leaves it with whoever already has it.

trophy.name: The Axe
trophy.text: Sources disagree on how many times it has been stolen since 1933: one counts three Cal thefts and four Stanford ones, ending in 1973, another nine in all since 1899. A 1978 fake-Axe stunt led some papers to report a theft that did not happen.

sources.label: A brief history of the Stanford Axe, Sports Illustrated
Traditions of the Big Game, Berkeley

ucla|usc.title: Victory Bell
ucla|usc.summary: UCLA's bell, stolen by USC students in 1941, became the prize of the city's biggest game.
origin: The 295-pound brass bell came off a Southern Pacific locomotive. The UCLA Alumni Association gave it to the school in 1939, and for two seasons cheerleaders rang it after each Bruin point.
At UCLA's opening game of 1941, six members of USC's Sigma Phi Epsilon fraternity infiltrated the Bruin rooting section and helped load the bell onto a truck. It was hidden for more than a year.
Since 1942 the winner of the game has been awarded the bell, and by tradition the winner paints it in its own colors.

trophy.name: Victory Bell
trophy.text: A 295-pound brass bell, painted in the colors of whichever school holds it.

sources.label: History of the Victory Bell, Daily Bruin

arkansas|lsu.title: Battle for the Golden Boot
arkansas|lsu.summary: Arkansas and LSU have played since 1901 and since 1996 for a boot shaped like the two states.
origin: The series began in 1901, an LSU 15–0 win.
Former Arkansas linebacker and businessman David Bazzel created the Golden Boot in 1996. The first game played for it was November 20, 1996, at War Memorial Stadium in Little Rock, and LSU won.

trophy.name: Golden Boot
trophy.text: A 24-karat gold boot of about 200 pounds (some sources say 175) valued at around $10,000, shaped like the outline of Arkansas and Louisiana together. It is among the heaviest trophies in college football.

sources.label: The history behind the Arkansas–LSU Boot, Whole Hog Sports
A quick history of the Battle for the Boot, LSU Rivals
How the Golden Boot began, The Reveille

arizona|arizona-state.title: The Territorial Cup
arizona|arizona-state.summary: Arizona and Arizona State play for the oldest rivalry trophy in college football, named for the days when Arizona was a territory.
origin: The first game was Thanksgiving Day, November 30, 1899, in Tucson: Arizona State, then the Tempe Normal School, won 11–2 in front of a reported 300 fans. Arizona did not become a state until 1912, hence 'Territorial'.

The cup was awarded that year to the winner of the Territorial Football League. It then went missing for about 80 years and was found in 1980 at ASU (one ASU account says in the Alumni Association's basement, another in a vault). The NCAA authenticated it as the original.
Since 2001 or 2002 it has been a traveling trophy, displayed by each year's winner.

trophy.name: Territorial Cup
trophy.text: A silver cup, recognized as the oldest rivalry trophy in college football. Since 2009–10 a separate series trophy goes to the school with the most head-to-head wins across 20 sports.

sources.label: Territorial Cup history and traditions, Arizona Alumni
The Territorial Cup, Sun Devil Athletics
The intense history of the Territorial Cup, ABC15

smu|tcu.title: Battle for the Iron Skillet
smu|tcu.summary: SMU and TCU have played since 1915, and since 1946 for a frying pan that was meant to stop vandalism.
origin: The teams first met in 1915, in the season opener in Fort Worth. The first game for the Iron Skillet was November 30, 1946, with SMU winning.

The two schools tell different stories about why a skillet. TCU's account is that the SMU student council proposed a trophy, TCU agreed, and the skillet was chosen for reasons history books do not record. SMU's account credits a fan who fried frog legs as a joke before the game. A 1946 Dallas Morning News story gave a practical reason: to curb the 'mutilation of school property' by rowdy fans, after more than $1,000 of damage to both campuses the year before.
The original skillet was later lost, and the current one is a replacement; sources give 1993 for it.

trophy.name: Iron Skillet
trophy.text: A cast-iron skillet that goes to the winner each year.

sources.label: A look back at the Iron Skillet rivalry, Texas Football
Battle of the Iron Skillet, FOX 4

nevada|unlv.title: The Battle for Nevada · Fremont Cannon
nevada|unlv.summary: Nevada and UNLV play for a replica cannon that is painted in the winner's colors.
origin: The Fremont Cannon is a replica of the mountain howitzer explorer John C. Fremont abandoned in the Sierra Nevada in a snowstorm (sources give 1843 or 1844). Kennecott Copper donated the money to build it.

It was built in 1970 (one account says it was completed in 1969, and sources disagree on which school held it first). It weighs about 545 pounds and cost about $10,000, and is described as the heaviest and most expensive trophy in college football.

It used to be fired after scores. It has not been since Rebel players and fans accidentally dropped it while hoisting it in celebration, in 1999 or 2000. The winner paints it in its colors: red for UNLV, blue for Nevada.

trophy.name: Fremont Cannon
trophy.text: A replica mountain howitzer, painted the color of whichever school holds it.

indiana|michigan-state.title: The Old Brass Spittoon
indiana|michigan-state.summary: Indiana and Michigan State have played for an antique spittoon since 1950.
origin: Michigan State won the first game for it in 1950, 35–0. Indiana first won it in 1958, 6–0.

Accounts of how the spittoon was found differ. One credits Gene McDermott, a Michigan State class president, who bought it at an antique shop (one source says in Lansing, for $50). The trophy was made official by a telegram to the Indiana student senate.

trophy.name: Old Brass Spittoon
trophy.text: An antique brass spittoon passed between the schools.

sources.label: Old Brass Spittoon history, Indiana Daily Student
Inside the Brass Spittoon rivalry, Indiana Athletics

illinois|ohio-state.title: The Illibuck Trophy
illinois|ohio-state.summary: Illinois and Ohio State began playing for a live turtle in 1925, and the trophy is now a wooden one.
origin: In 1925 two junior honor societies, Ohio State's Bucket and Dipper and Illinois' Atius-Sachem, agreed to create a trophy passed between them. The first trophy was a living turtle named Illibuck.
The turtle died in 1926. Ohio State is remembered for 'avenging' its death by winning at Champaign that year.
The replacement is a carved wooden turtle. There have been ten of them in the century since, each with the scores of the games carved into its shell.

trophy.name: Illibuck
trophy.text: A carved wooden turtle. Illibuck is the second-oldest trophy tradition in the Big Ten; only the Little Brown Jug, first awarded in 1903, is older.

sources.label: So what is the Illibuck anyway? The Champaign Room
Ohio State avenged the death of Illibuck, Eleven Warriors

iowa-state|missouri.title: The Telephone Trophy
iowa-state|missouri.summary: Iowa State and Missouri play for an old rotary telephone, though nobody agrees on how that began.
origin: The trophy has been awarded to the winner since 1959, according to the sources found. How it began is disputed: one version ties it to a 1959 game in Ames and Northwestern Bell Telephone Company of Ames; an Associated Press column from 2010 says the alumni chapters of the two schools met in Chicago in 1925 and decided on a trophy. Neither could be confirmed against a clean primary source.

trophy.name: Telephone Trophy
trophy.text: An old rotary telephone on a tall wooden base. The receiver is painted half gold, for Missouri, and half red, for Iowa State, and a plate on the base records each game's result.

sources.label: Cyclones hoping to use the Telephone for another year, Iowa State Daily
Telephone Trophy adds incentive, Southeast Missourian
